content: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by reversible airway narrowing due to bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and mucus production. Despite advances in treatment, asthma remains a significant cause of preventable illness and death. Effective self-management, guided by healthcare professionals, is essential to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. Modern telephone and internet-based technologies now allow patients to monitor their lung function and asthma symptoms at home. This data can be electronically shared with healthcare providers, enabling feedback and intervention between clinic visits. Such technological approaches aim to improve health outcomes and reduce the need for emergency care in individuals with asthma and other chronic conditions. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of home telemonitoring combined with healthcare professional feedback, compared to standard care. Researchers conducted a comprehensive search of clinical trials up to May 2016, using databases such as the Cochrane Airways Review Group Specialised Register, clinicaltrials.gov, and the World Health Organization trials portal. They also reviewed reference lists of other studies and contacted trial authors for additional information. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults or children with asthma, where technology was used to monitor and share asthma-related data with healthcare providers. Studies were excluded if the technology was used solely for monitoring without input from a healthcare professional. A total of 18 studies involving 2,268 participants were included in the analysis. These studies primarily involved individuals with mild to moderate persistent asthma and followed them for durations ranging from three to 12 months. Participants in the intervention group used various technologies, such as text messaging, web-based systems, or phone calls, to record and share their symptoms. This group was compared to participants receiving usual care or a control intervention. The evidence did not clearly demonstrate whether telemonitoring with healthcare feedback reduced the likelihood of asthma exacerbations requiring oral steroids (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.44; 466 participants; four studies), emergency department visits (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.58; 1,018 participants; eight studies), or hospitalizations (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.49; 1,042 participants; 10 studies) compared to usual care. The confidence in these findings was limited due to imprecision in the primary outcomes. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low. None of the studies separately reported serious or non-serious adverse events unrelated to asthma exacerbations. Evidence regarding asthma control measures was inconsistent and imprecise. There was a potential, albeit small, benefit for quality of life (MD 0.23, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.45; 796 participants; six studies; I² = 54%), but the effect size was minimal, and study results varied. Telemonitoring interventions may offer some additional benefit for certain lung function measures, but these findings are uncertain due to potential biases. The authors concluded that current evidence does not support the widespread adoption of telemonitoring with healthcare provider feedback between asthma clinic visits. The studies reviewed did not demonstrate that telemonitoring strategies significantly improve symptom control or reduce the need for oral steroids compared to usual care. Additionally, the potential for unintended harms has not been ruled out. While small improvements in quality of life were observed, these findings are subject to bias due to the unblinded nature of the studies. Similarly, any observed benefits in lung function are uncertain due to possible attrition bias. Larger, pragmatic studies involving both children and adults are needed to better assess the real-world benefits of telemonitoring interventions in preventing asthma exacerbations and avoiding potential harms. The generalizability of the current findings is limited, as the observed benefits may be partially attributed to the increased attention participants received during clinical trials. Future research could benefit from qualitative studies exploring patient and provider preferences or identifying subgroups of patients, such as those with frequent asthma attacks, who may derive greater benefit from closer monitoring.
